description: A Study says what to solve - stationary, time dependent, frequency domain, eigenfrequency - and its Study Extensions add sweeps and batch/cluster execution. Each study owns a Solver Configurations branch whose Solution node holds the low-level sequence: Compile Equations, Dependent Variables, the stationary/time-dependent/eigenvalue solver, the nonlinear method (Fully Coupled or Segregated) and the linear solver (Direct or Iterative with a preconditioner). In the COMSOL API for Java study steps are created with model.study("std1").create(tag, type) and solver features with model.sol("sol1").create(tag, type).

tools.name: Stationary
tools.description: Study step for a steady-state problem: the time derivatives are dropped and a stationary solver finds the equilibrium solution. It is the starting point for static structural analysis, steady heat transfer, DC conduction, electrostatics and steady laminar flow, and it is also used as the first step of a prestressed or linearized analysis. Its Study Extensions section carries the auxiliary sweep (continuation), and the Adaptive Mesh Refinement and error estimation settings live here too.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Study Steps > Stationary > Stationary (or Add Study > Stationary when creating the study)

parameters.name: geometricNonlinearity
parameters.description: Boolean. Include geometric nonlinearity (large deformation). Requires Structural Mechanics, Acoustics, MEMS or Multibody Dynamics Module.

parameters.name: useparam
parameters.description: on | off. Enable the auxiliary sweep (continuation) in Study Extensions.

parameters.name: pname / plistarr / punit
parameters.description: Auxiliary-sweep parameter names, value lists (one row per name) and units.

parameters.name: sweeptype
parameters.description: filled | sparse (default sparse). Solve every combination of the parameter lists, or the tuples formed column by column.

parameters.name: solnum / notlistsolnum
parameters.description: Which solution to take initial values from (auto | first | last | interp | manual | index), and which solution supplies values for variables not solved for.

parameters.name: useadvanceddisable
parameters.description: on | off. Turn on the Physics and Variables Selection list so individual physics interfaces or features can be disabled in this step.

tools.notes: A nonlinear stationary problem that will not converge from the default initial guess is usually fixed by ramping a load or a material nonlinearity with the auxiliary sweep and continuation, which reuses the previous solution as the next initial guess. Adding Stationary steps in sequence (with Values of Dependent Variables set to the previous step) is the standard way to build prestressed and multi-stage analyses.

tools.name: Time Dependent
tools.description: Study step for transient simulations: the solver integrates the equations over a list of times using an implicit method (BDF by default, generalized alpha as an alternative). Use it for transient heat conduction, transient flow, charging and discharging, moving loads, and any problem where the initial condition matters. The Times field is only the list of output times - the solver picks its own internal steps unless you constrain it in the Time-Dependent Solver node.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Study Steps > Time Dependent > Time Dependent

parameters.name: tlist
parameters.description: Time list, normally written as range(0,0.1,10) or an explicit vector with units, e.g. range(0,0.01,1)[s].

parameters.name: useparam / pname / plistarr / punit
parameters.description: Auxiliary sweep over parameters on top of the time integration.

parameters.name: solnum / notlistsolnum
parameters.description: Initial values taken from a previous solution (auto | first | last | interp | manual | index) and the solution used for variables not solved for.

parameters.name: useadvanceddisable
parameters.description: on | off. Expose the Physics and Variables Selection list for this step.

tools.notes: The API type string is "Transient", not "TimeDependent". Output times do not control accuracy: to force the solver to resolve a fast transient, set Time stepping to Intermediate or Strict in the Time-Dependent Solver node, or lower its relative tolerance. Storing hundreds of output times of a large 3D model can make the .mph file enormous - store fewer times or use Store Solution selectively.

tools.name: Frequency Domain
tools.description: Study step that computes the steady harmonic response of a linear or linearized model at one or more frequencies, solving a complex-valued problem per frequency. It is the standard step for AC circuits, electromagnetic wave propagation, acoustics, frequency response of structures and impedance analysis. The related Frequency-Domain Perturbation step (type "Frequencylinearized") linearizes about a bias solution for small-signal analysis.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Study Steps > Frequency Domain > Frequency Domain

parameters.name: plist
parameters.description: List of frequencies, e.g. range(100,10,2000) or 10^{range(1,0.1,6)} for a logarithmic sweep.

parameters.name: punit
parameters.description: Frequency unit, default Hz.

parameters.name: preusesol
parameters.description: no | yes | auto. Reuse the solution from the previous frequency as the initial guess.

parameters.name: solnum / notlistsolnum
parameters.description: Linearization point / initial values taken from another step's solution, and the solution used for variables not solved for.

tools.notes: Each frequency is an independent linear solve, so a frequency sweep parallelizes well and is a natural candidate for a Parametric Sweep with a cluster. For strongly resonant systems, a modal step (Frequency Domain, Modal, built on an Eigenfrequency step) is far cheaper than a full sweep. Time-domain results can be converted with the Time to Frequency FFT study step (type "TimeToFreqFFT") and back with Frequency to Time FFT.

tools.name: Eigenfrequency
tools.description: Computes the natural frequencies and mode shapes of a linear or linearized model by solving an eigenvalue problem, reporting results directly as frequencies rather than raw eigenvalues. Use it for structural modal analysis, acoustic cavity modes, resonator design and as the basis of any modal-superposition (Frequency Domain, Modal) analysis. The search is controlled by the desired number of eigenfrequencies and a shift that tells the solver roughly where to look.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Study Steps > Eigenfrequency > Eigenfrequency

parameters.name: neigs
parameters.description: Desired number of eigenfrequencies (default 6).

parameters.name: shift
parameters.description: Complex scalar shift - the frequency the search is centred on. Set it near the band of interest; 0 finds the lowest modes.

parameters.name: appnreigs
parameters.description: Approximate number of eigenfrequencies (default 20) when searching a region rather than around a shift.

parameters.name: useparam / pname / plistarr
parameters.description: Auxiliary sweep, for example to track how modes shift with a geometric or material parameter.

tools.notes: A structure with free boundaries has rigid-body modes at (numerically) zero frequency; set a nonzero shift to skip them. Prestress effects need a Stationary step first plus a Prestressed Analysis, Eigenfrequency setup. The underlying solver node exposes the ARPACK/FEAST choice and the search region.

tools.name: Eigenvalue
tools.description: The general form of the eigenvalue study step: it returns raw eigenvalues (lambda) instead of frequencies, which is what you want for buckling factors, propagation constants, growth rates in stability analysis and general PDE eigenproblems. Settings mirror the Eigenfrequency step - number of eigenvalues, search shift, optional search region - but no frequency conversion is applied. Choose it whenever the eigenvalue has a physical meaning other than a frequency.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Study Steps > Eigenvalue > Eigenvalue

parameters.name: neigs
parameters.description: Desired number of eigenvalues (default 6).

parameters.name: shift
parameters.description: Complex scalar giving the point in the complex plane the search is centred on.

parameters.name: useparam / pname / plistarr
parameters.description: Auxiliary sweep over parameters while computing eigenvalues.

parameters.name: solnum / notlistsolnum
parameters.description: Linearization point and values for variables not solved for, taken from an earlier step.

tools.notes: Linear Buckling analysis is built on an eigenvalue solve of the prestressed stiffness: add a Stationary step with the unit load, then a Linear Buckling step (Structural Mechanics Module), and read the critical load factor from the eigenvalue. Nonlinear eigenvalue problems are handled by the arpacknonlinear option on the Eigenvalue Solver node.

tools.name: Parametric Sweep
tools.description: A study extension that re-solves the entire study for every value in one or more parameter lists, storing one solution per parameter set. Use it for design studies, material comparisons, geometry variations and any scan where each run is independent. Unlike the auxiliary sweep, a parametric sweep can change geometry parameters (the geometry and mesh are rebuilt), and its runs can be distributed with Batch Sweep or Cluster Sweep.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Parametric Sweep (add parameter names and value lists in the settings table)

parameters.name: pname
parameters.description: Vector of parameter names to vary (they must exist under Global Definitions > Parameters).

parameters.name: plistarr
parameters.description: Real matrix of parameter values, one row of values per parameter name.

parameters.name: sweeptype
parameters.description: filled | sparse | switch (default sparse). All combinations, matching tuples column by column, or a switch-style sweep.

parameters.name: keepsol
parameters.description: last | all. Store every parameter's solution or only the last one - the main control over .mph file size.

parameters.name: plot / plotgroup
parameters.description: on | off, and which plot group to update while solving.

parameters.name: probesel / probes
parameters.description: all | none | manual, and the probes to evaluate during the sweep.

parameters.name: reusesol
parameters.description: Reuse the solution from the previous parameter value as the initial guess for the next one.

tools.notes: sparse requires all rows of plistarr to have the same length and pairs them element by element; filled solves the full Cartesian product, which grows fast with two or three parameters. A parametric sweep restarts each run from the default initial conditions, so it is not a continuation method - use the auxiliary sweep when each run should start from the previous solution. The solutions end up in a solution group; model.batch("p1").feature(...).getString("psol") finds the container holding them.

tools.name: Auxiliary Sweep (Continuation)
tools.description: The sweep built into a study step's Study Extensions section: the same discretized problem is solved for a list of parameter values, and with continuation turned on each solve starts from the previous solution. This is the standard remedy for a nonlinear stationary problem that will not converge - ramp the load, the nonlinearity or a material property from a value that does converge up to the target. It is implemented by a Parametric attribute on the stationary solver, so it never rebuilds geometry or mesh.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Stationary > Settings > Study Extensions > Auxiliary sweep (equivalently Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Stationary Solver 1 > right-click > Parametric)

parameters.name: useparam (study step)
parameters.description: on | off. Switches the auxiliary sweep on for that step.

parameters.name: pname / plistarr / punit (study step)
parameters.description: Parameter names, value lists and units for the sweep.

parameters.name: sweeptype
parameters.description: sparse (tuples column by column) or filled (all combinations).

parameters.name: pcontinuationmode (solver Parametric attribute)
parameters.description: no | last | manual (default last). Which parameter is used for continuation - last means the last name in pname.

parameters.name: plot / probesel
parameters.description: Plot while solving and choose which probes are evaluated at each parameter value.

tools.notes: Auxiliary sweep versus Parametric Sweep: the auxiliary sweep is inside one solver call, keeps geometry and mesh fixed, and supports continuation; the Parametric Sweep re-runs the whole study (so it can vary geometry parameters) but restarts each solve. If a nonlinear model diverges, ramping with a finer parameter list is usually more effective than loosening the tolerance.

tools.name: Batch
tools.description: A study extension that hands the current study to a separate COMSOL batch process on the same machine instead of solving in the interactive session. The GUI stays responsive, the batch run writes its own model file, and the solution is read back when it finishes. Use it for long runs you do not want to block the desktop on, and the related Batch Sweep to run the parameter sets of a parametric sweep as several concurrent batch processes.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Batch (or Batch Sweep); the created job appears under Study 1 > Job Configurations

parameters.name: batchfile
parameters.description: Name of the batch model file written by the run (default batchmodel.mph).

parameters.name: Job Configurations
parameters.description: The generated External Process / Batch node holds the COMSOL executable path, working directory, number of cores and the command-line arguments used for the run.

parameters.name: Specify filenames
parameters.description: Output model, status and log filenames, so several concurrent jobs do not overwrite each other.

tools.notes: Batch Sweep (type "BatchSweep") is the parallel version: it splits a parametric sweep into independent batch processes, which is the fastest way to use many cores when each run is small. A study can have only one attached solver sequence but several batch features. The equivalent outside the GUI is comsol batch -inputfile model.mph -outputfile out.mph.

tools.name: Cluster Computing
tools.description: A study extension that submits the study as a COMSOL batch job to a job scheduler (Slurm, PBS, OGS/GE, HPCS/HPC Pack) or to a plain list of hosts, so the model is solved on a cluster with distributed (MPI) memory. Use it when one model is too large for a single machine's RAM, and Cluster Sweep when many independent parameter runs should be spread over the cluster. The settings mirror the comsol -nn / -nnhost / -f hostfile command-line options.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Cluster Computing (Preferences > Multicore and Cluster Computing sets the defaults); Cluster Sweep is added the same way

parameters.name: batchfile
parameters.description: Name of the batch model file submitted to the scheduler (default batchmodel.mph).

parameters.name: Scheduler type
parameters.description: General, Slurm, PBS, OGS/GE, HPCS or Not distributed, selected in the node settings; each exposes its own queue/account/directory fields.

parameters.name: Number of nodes / cores per node
parameters.description: Distributed node count and the cores used on each - the GUI equivalent of -nn and -nnhost.

parameters.name: batchlic
parameters.description: on | off. Whether the batch job checks out its own license.

tools.notes: Distributed parallelism helps most when the bottleneck is memory (a direct factorization that does not fit in RAM) or when many parameter values can run independently; a single small model usually runs faster on one shared-memory node. Cluster Sweep (type "ClusterSweep") distributes parameter sets rather than splitting one solve. Check the floating network license terms before requesting many nodes.

tools.name: Optimization
tools.description: Solver feature that solves a PDE-constrained optimization problem: it drives design variables (from Optimization features in Definitions or a physics interface) to minimize an objective subject to constraints, calling the underlying stationary or time-dependent solver for each design iteration. Gradient-based solvers (SNOPT, MMA, IPOPT, Levenberg-Marquardt) need analytic or adjoint sensitivities and converge in few iterations; gradient-free solvers (BOBYQA, COBYLA, Nelder-Mead, coordinate search, Monte Carlo) need no derivatives but many more model evaluations. The computed solution holds the model evaluated at the optimal design.
tools.usage: Study 1 > right-click > Optimization (Optimization Module), which adds the Optimization solver under Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1

parameters.name: optmethod
parameters.description: neldermead | bobyqa | cobyla | ego | ipopt | gcmma | mma | lm (COMSOL 6.4).

parameters.name: Solver attribute
parameters.description: Add StationaryAttrib for a stationary forward problem or TimeAttrib for a time-dependent one under the Optimization feature.

parameters.name: Objective and control variables
parameters.description: Defined by Optimization nodes in the model (Global Objective, Integral Objective, Control Variable Field, Global Control Variables) rather than on the solver.

tools.notes: Requires the Optimization Module. Parameter estimation and least-squares fitting to measured data use the same feature with an experimental-data objective. The related Sensitivity study step and Sensitivity solver feature compute derivatives of an objective with respect to parameters without running a full optimization. COMSOL 6.4 removed SNOPT: the study step setting is optmethod = neldermead | bobyqa | cobyla | ego | ipopt | gcmma | mma | lm (older optsolver/snopt calls are migrated to ipopt).

tools.name: Compute (model.study("std1").run())
tools.description: Runs a study: rebuilds the geometry and mesh if they are out of date, generates or updates the default solver sequence if needed, and executes every study step in order. This is the API equivalent of pressing Compute on a Study node and is the single call that most scripts end with. Use setGenConv to control whether convergence plots are generated while solving.
tools.usage: model.study("std1").run(); GUI: Study 1 > right-click > Compute (F8)

parameters.name: run()
parameters.description: Runs the whole study, creating the default solver sequence if none exists.

parameters.name: setGenConv(boolean)
parameters.description: Generate convergence plots while solving - the Convergence Plot group under Results that shows the error estimate per iteration.

parameters.name: Solver log
parameters.description: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Log, and the Progress and Log windows, show step size, Newton iterations and error estimates for a finished or running solve.

tools.notes: model.study("std1").run() regenerates a default solver sequence, so any manual solver edits can be overwritten; when you have hand-tuned the solver, call model.sol("sol1").runAll() instead. If a nonlinear solve fails, read the log: 'Undefined value found' points at a material or expression hole, while a stalled damping factor points at a bad initial guess and calls for continuation.

tools.name: Solution (sol)
tools.description: The Solution node under Solver Configurations is the container for the whole low-level solver sequence and for the computed data. createAutoSequence builds a default sequence for a study (Compile Equations, Dependent Variables, the solvers), runAll executes it, and run/runFrom/runFromTo execute part of it - invaluable when you want to re-run only the linear solve after changing a preconditioner. attach and study connect a sequence to the study whose steps it implements.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 (right-click for Compute, Compute to Selected, Get Initial Value, Update Solution); API: model.sol().create("sol1")

parameters.name: createAutoSequence(<stag>)
parameters.description: Generate the default solver sequence for a study, e.g. model.sol().createAutoSequence("std1").

parameters.name: attach(<stag>) / study(<stag>)
parameters.description: Attach the solver sequence to a study and set the study it belongs to.

parameters.name: runAll()
parameters.description: Run every feature of the sequence - the equivalent of Compute on the Solution node.

parameters.name: run(<ftag>) / runFrom(<ftag>) / runFromTo(<start>,<stop>)
parameters.description: Run up to a feature, from a feature onwards, or between two features.

parameters.name: continueRun()
parameters.description: Resume an interrupted or stopped computation from where it left off.

tools.notes: Each study has exactly one attached solver sequence (but may own several batch features). Get Initial Value runs the sequence far enough to evaluate initial conditions without solving - the fastest way to check materials, coupling expressions and selections before committing to a long run. All run methods take an optional createPlots boolean.

tools.name: Compile Equations
tools.description: The first node of a solver sequence (API type "StudyStep"). It holds a reference to a study and to one of its steps and, when run, compiles the corresponding low-level equation representation - the discretized system that the following features operate on. Every time you change physics, selections or the mesh, this node is what regenerates the underlying problem, and its Physics and Variables Selection determines which interfaces take part.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Compile Equations; API: model.sol("sol1").create("st1", "StudyStep")

parameters.name: study / studystep
parameters.description: Tags of the study and of the study step whose problem definition is compiled.

parameters.name: useent / entsel
parameters.description: Restrict the compiled problem to the geometric entities of named selections.

parameters.name: partmethod
parameters.description: parent | mo | nd | wnd | false. Domain partitioning method for distributed (cluster) computing: inherit, mesh ordering, nested dissection, weighted nested dissection or off.

parameters.name: keeplog
parameters.description: Boolean. Keep warnings emitted during compilation in the stored log.

tools.notes: A solver sequence normally contains one Compile Equations node per study step; multi-step studies produce several, each followed by its own solver. Errors about undefined variables or missing material properties surface here rather than in the solver, because this is where the equations are assembled symbolically.

tools.name: Dependent Variables
tools.description: Solver node (API type "Variables") that controls initial values for the variables being solved for, how variables not solved for are computed, and the scaling of each field. Its Field and State subnodes are created automatically from the compiled problem. Scaling matters: when fields of wildly different magnitudes are solved together (pressure in Pa and displacement in microns), manual scaling often decides whether the Newton solver converges at all.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Dependent Variables 1 (expand for one Field node per dependent variable); API: model.sol("sol1").create("v1", "Variables")

parameters.name: Initial values
parameters.description: Initial expression, or values taken from a stored solution - the GUI's Values of variables not solved for / Initial values of variables solved for.

parameters.name: Field subnodes
parameters.description: One per dependent variable; carry the scaling method (automatic, manual, none, initial value based) and the manual scale value.

parameters.name: clist / cname
parameters.description: Constant names and values supplied as input parameters to the solver sequence.

parameters.name: updateVariables()
parameters.description: Method that forces a manual refresh of the Field/State subnodes after the problem changes.

tools.notes: If the Analysis of the sequence changes, the Field attributes are regenerated, so scripts should not assume fixed subnode tags. A relative tolerance is measured against the scale of each field, which is why a badly scaled field can be reported as converged while still being wrong; set manual scaling to the expected magnitude of the solution when in doubt.

tools.name: Stationary Solver
tools.description: The operation feature that actually solves a steady-state problem, optionally with parameter stepping, mesh adaptation, sensitivity or optimization attributes. It owns the relative tolerance and the choice of running the nonlinear (Newton) solver or treating the problem as linear, and it holds the nonlinear method (Fully Coupled or Segregated) and the linear solver as child attributes. Tuning starts here: relative tolerance for accuracy, nonlin for whether Newton runs at all, and the child attributes for robustness and memory.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Stationary Solver 1; API: model.sol("sol1").create("s1", "Stationary")

parameters.name: stol
parameters.description: Relative tolerance (default 1e-3) when control is user. Tighten to 1e-6 for accuracy studies, loosen for a quick look.

parameters.name: nonlin
parameters.description: auto | on | off | linper. Force the nonlinear solver on or off, or select linear perturbation.

parameters.name: control
parameters.description: Tag of the controlling study step, or user when the node is edited manually (editing a field in the GUI sets this automatically).

parameters.name: plot / plotgroup
parameters.description: Plot while solving and which plot group to refresh.

parameters.name: linpmethod / linpsol / linpsolnum
parameters.description: Linearization point settings for perturbation and linearized analyses.

parameters.name: Attributes
parameters.description: Create Fully Coupled or Segregated for the nonlinear method, Direct or Iterative for the linear solver, and Parametric for continuation.

tools.notes: The default sequence already contains a nonlinear method (tag fcDef or similar) and a default linear solver; adding your own attribute means you should remove or ignore the default one (feature().remove("fcDef")). When a stationary solve diverges, the productive order is: check the initial guess, add continuation, switch Fully Coupled to Segregated (or back), then change the linear solver.

tools.name: Time-Dependent Solver
tools.description: The operation feature (API type "Time") that integrates a transient problem. BDF (variable order 1-5) is the default and is robust and dissipative, which suits parabolic problems such as heat transfer and diffusion; generalized alpha is second-order with controllable numerical damping and is preferred for structural dynamics and wave-like problems. The time-stepping mode decides how much freedom the solver has relative to the output time list, and the relative tolerance controls the local error per step.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Time-Dependent Solver 1; API: model.sol("sol1").create("t1", "Time")

parameters.name: tlist
parameters.description: List of output times, normally inherited from the study step, e.g. range(0,0.05,2).

parameters.name: timemethod
parameters.description: bdf | genalpha | init. Implicit time-stepping method (default bdf).

parameters.name: tstepsbdf / tstepsgenalpha
parameters.description: free | intermediate | strict | manual (default free). Free lets the solver step past output times and interpolate; intermediate forces at least one step between outputs; strict forces a step exactly at every output time.

parameters.name: rtol
parameters.description: Relative tolerance (default 0.01). The main accuracy control - tighten to 1e-3 or 1e-4 when the transient matters.

parameters.name: maxorder
parameters.description: Maximum BDF order, 1-5 (default 5). Lowering to 2 adds damping and can stabilize a stiff or oscillatory problem.

parameters.name: tout
parameters.description: tlist | tsteps | tstepsclosest. Store the output times by interpolation, every step the solver takes, or the steps closest to the output times.

parameters.name: atolglobal / atolglobalfactor / atolmethod
parameters.description: Absolute tolerance, globally or per field, which governs fields whose values pass through zero.

tools.notes: Free time stepping with widely spaced output times can step straight over a short pulse; use Intermediate or Strict when a source changes faster than the output interval. BDF of order 5 is only weakly damped and can ring on discontinuous inputs - lower maxorder or switch to generalized alpha. Events (implicit/explicit Event features) and Stop Conditions both attach to this solver.

tools.name: Eigenvalue Solver
tools.description: The operation feature that solves the discretized eigenvalue problem for an Eigenfrequency, Eigenvalue, Linear Buckling or Boundary Mode Analysis step. ARPACK (shift-and-invert Arnoldi) is the default and finds a requested number of eigenvalues near a shift; FEAST computes all eigenvalues inside a contour in the complex plane and parallelizes well over a wide band; LAPACK solves small dense problems completely. Nonlinear eigenvalue problems are reduced to a quadratic approximation around a reference value or handled by the ARPACK nonlinear option.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Eigenvalue Solver 1; API: model.sol("sol1").create("e1", "Eigenvalue")

parameters.name: eigsolver
parameters.description: arpack | feast | lapack | arpacknonlinear (default arpack).

parameters.name: neigs
parameters.description: Number of eigenvalues sought with ARPACK (default 6).

parameters.name: shift
parameters.description: Eigenvalue search location for ARPACK or LAPACK (default 0).

parameters.name: eigwhich
parameters.description: lm | lr | sr | li | si (default lm). Search direction: largest magnitude, largest/smallest real part, largest/smallest imaginary part.

parameters.name: eigmethod
parameters.description: manual | region. Search around a shift, or inside a rectangular region of the complex plane (ARPACK).

parameters.name: eigunit
parameters.description: Unit for the reported eigenvalue (default rad/s).

parameters.name: conmid / conrad / conlbdy
parameters.description: Contour centre, radius and interval bounds when eigsolver is feast.

parameters.name: transform
parameters.description: Eigenvalue transformation applied before reporting (for example to frequency).

tools.notes: Shift-and-invert requires factorizing (K - sigma*M) once per shift, so the eigenvalue solver is almost always paired with a direct linear solver and is memory-bound in 3D. Asking for many eigenvalues far from the shift is slow - use several shifts or FEAST with a contour covering the band. A shift exactly on an eigenvalue makes the shifted matrix singular; nudge it.

tools.name: Fully Coupled
tools.description: The nonlinear method that forms one Jacobian for all dependent variables and solves the complete coupled system with a damped Newton method at every iteration. It gives quadratic convergence near the solution and is the right choice for strongly coupled problems (thermal-structural, fluid-structure interaction, electrochemistry) and for any model where a segregated split stalls. The price is memory: the Jacobian contains every coupling block, so a fully coupled 3D multiphysics problem can be several times larger than a segregated one.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Stationary Solver 1 > right-click > Fully Coupled; API: model.sol("sol1").feature("s1").create("fc1", "FullyCoupled")

parameters.name: dtech
parameters.description: const | auto | bcktrack | hnlin | ddog. Damping technique: constant damping, automatic, backtracking, automatic highly nonlinear, or double dogleg. Default auto (const for time-dependent).

parameters.name: damp
parameters.description: Damping factor for the damped Newton method (default 1). Values around 0.1-0.5 with dtech const help very nonlinear problems start.

parameters.name: maxiter
parameters.description: Maximum number of Newton iterations (default 25; 4 inside a time-dependent solver).

parameters.name: jtech
parameters.description: minimal | once | onevery. How often the Jacobian is recomputed - onevery is the most robust, minimal the cheapest.

parameters.name: ntolfact
parameters.description: Tolerance factor multiplying the solver's relative tolerance for the nonlinear convergence check.

parameters.name: stabacc
parameters.description: Stabilization and acceleration, including pseudo time stepping (cflcmp) for stationary flow problems and Anderson acceleration (aacc).

parameters.name: linsolver
parameters.description: Tag of the linear solver attribute (Direct or Iterative) used for each Newton step.

tools.notes: Automatic highly nonlinear (hnlin) starts with heavy damping and relaxes it, which rescues many models that stall with the plain automatic technique. If the damping factor collapses towards zero over successive iterations, the problem is the initial guess or the model, not the solver - add continuation. Fully Coupled and Segregated are mutually exclusive on one solver node.

tools.name: Segregated
tools.description: The nonlinear method that splits the dependent variables into groups and solves each group in turn while holding the others fixed, iterating (nonlinear Uzawa iterations) until all groups converge. Each Segregated Step owns its own variable group and linear solver, so memory per solve is far smaller than for a fully coupled Jacobian - this is why large CFD, turbulence and Joule-heating models default to it. The trade-off is slower (linear rather than quadratic) convergence and possible stalling when the coupling between groups is strong.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Stationary Solver 1 > right-click > Segregated, then Segregated 1 > right-click > Segregated Step; API: model.sol("sol1").feature("s1").create("se1", "Segregated")

parameters.name: maxsegiter
parameters.description: Maximum number of segregated iterations (default 100; 25 in a time-dependent solver).

parameters.name: segterm
parameters.description: iter | tol | itertol (default tol). Terminate on a fixed iteration count, on tolerance, or on either.

parameters.name: segtermonres
parameters.description: off | on | auto | both. Whether convergence is judged on the solution, the residual, or both.

parameters.name: ntolfact
parameters.description: Tolerance factor applied to the solver's relative tolerance.

parameters.name: segstabacc
parameters.description: none | segclfcmp | segaacc. No stabilization, pseudo time stepping for stationary problems, or Anderson acceleration.

parameters.name: SegregatedStep subnodes
parameters.description: One per variable group (create(fname, "SegregatedStep")), each with segvar/segcomp (the fields in the group), linsolver (its linear solver tag) and maxsubiter (maximum substep iterations, default 20).

parameters.name: ratelimit / ratelimitactive
parameters.description: Limit on the nonlinear convergence rate, used to detect a stalled segregated iteration.

tools.notes: Choose Segregated when the fully coupled Jacobian does not fit in memory or when the physics are only weakly coupled (flow then temperature, EM then heat); choose Fully Coupled when the segregated iteration stalls or oscillates, which is the classic symptom of strong two-way coupling. Grouping matters: variables that are tightly coupled to each other (velocity and pressure) belong in the same segregated step. LumpedStep, LowerLimit and UpperLimit are additional subattributes of the segregated solver.

tools.name: Direct
tools.description: Linear system solver attribute that computes an LU (or Cholesky-like) factorization of the assembled matrix. It is robust - it solves anything nonsingular without tuning, needs no preconditioner and is reusable across right-hand sides - which makes it the default in 1D/2D and for eigenvalue and small 3D problems. Its cost is memory: fill-in makes the factors far denser than the matrix, so large 3D models eventually run out of RAM and must move to an iterative solver.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Stationary Solver 1 > right-click > Direct; API: model.sol("sol1").feature("s1").create("d1", "Direct")

parameters.name: linsolver
parameters.description: mumps | pardiso | spooles | dense (default mumps). MUMPS handles out-of-core and cluster (distributed) factorization; PARDISO is often fastest on one shared-memory machine; SPOOLES uses the least memory but is slower; dense is for small filled matrices.

parameters.name: ooc / oocmemory / memfracooc
parameters.description: Out-of-core operation (automatic | on | off) for MUMPS and PARDISO, with the in-core memory limit in MB - lets a factorization spill to disk instead of failing.

parameters.name: mumpsblr / mumpsblrtol
parameters.description: Block low-rank factorization for MUMPS and its tolerance (default 1e-8); a large memory and time saving on smooth 3D problems at slightly reduced accuracy.

parameters.name: pivotperturb / pivotstrategy / thresh
parameters.description: Pivot perturbation threshold, Bunch-Kaufman pivoting and pivot threshold - the knobs for nearly singular systems.

parameters.name: errorchk / iterrefine / maxrefinesteps
parameters.description: Error estimate checking and iterative refinement of the solution (default 15 refinement steps).

parameters.name: clusterpardiso
parameters.description: on | off. Use the Parallel Direct Sparse Solver for Clusters.

tools.notes: Rule of thumb: direct up to a few hundred thousand degrees of freedom in 3D, iterative beyond that. An 'out of memory during LU factorization' message means switch to PARDISO/MUMPS out-of-core, enable MUMPS block low-rank, or move to Iterative with a multigrid preconditioner. A Direct solver is also used as the coarse-grid solver inside Multigrid, where its memory cost is small.

tools.name: Iterative
tools.description: Linear system solver attribute that uses a Krylov subspace method and stops when the relative residual meets a tolerance, so memory stays close to the size of the matrix itself. GMRES is the general-purpose default; FGMRES allows a varying (flexible) preconditioner such as an inner iterative solve; BiCGStab is cheaper per iteration for nonsymmetric problems; Conjugate Gradients is the method of choice for symmetric positive definite systems such as static structural and Poisson problems. An iterative solver is only as good as its preconditioner - it always needs one.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Stationary Solver 1 > right-click > Iterative, then right-click the Iterative node to add a preconditioner; API: model.sol("sol1").feature("s1").create("i1", "Iterative")

parameters.name: linsolver
parameters.description: gmres | fgmres | bicgstab | tfqmr | cg | precond (default gmres). precond applies the preconditioner alone.

parameters.name: itrestart
parameters.description: Number of iterations before restart for GMRES/FGMRES (default 50). Larger keeps more Krylov vectors - better convergence, more memory.

parameters.name: maxlinit
parameters.description: Maximum number of linear iterations (default 10000).

parameters.name: rhob / errorchk
parameters.description: Factor in the linear error estimate and whether the error estimate is validated.

parameters.name: Preconditioner subfeature
parameters.description: Created on the Iterative node: "Multigrid" (geometric or algebraic), "IncompleteLU", "SAI", "Direct", plus SOR-family, Vanka, SCGS, domain decomposition and Krylov preconditioners.

parameters.name: droptol / droptype / fillratio
parameters.description: Incomplete LU controls: drop tolerance, dropping strategy (tol | fill) and fill ratio.

tools.notes: Use CG only for symmetric positive definite systems - applying it to a nonsymmetric problem silently misconverges. Stalling GMRES almost always means a poor preconditioner rather than a bad Krylov method: try a multigrid preconditioner before increasing the iteration count. Iterative solvers also interact with the nonlinear solver's adaptive tolerance, so an over-tight linear tolerance wastes time inside every Newton step.

tools.name: Multigrid
tools.description: The preconditioner (or standalone solver) that attacks the error on a hierarchy of coarser problems: cheap smoothers remove high-frequency error on each level and a coarse solve removes the smooth remainder. Geometric multigrid (gmg) coarsens the mesh or lowers the element order and is the fastest option for elliptic problems such as heat transfer, electrostatics and structural statics; algebraic multigrid (amg) builds the hierarchy from the matrix alone and needs no coarse mesh. Combined with GMRES or CG it gives near mesh-independent iteration counts, which is what makes very large 3D models solvable.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Stationary Solver 1 > Iterative 1 > right-click > Multigrid (then right-click Multigrid for Presmoother, Postsmoother and Coarse Solver settings)

parameters.name: prefun
parameters.description: gmg | amg | saamg. Geometric multigrid, algebraic multigrid or smoothed-aggregation AMG (default amg when used as a Krylov preconditioner, gmg otherwise).

parameters.name: mgcycle
parameters.description: v | w | f (default v). Multigrid cycle type; W and F cycles cost more per iteration but converge in fewer iterations on hard problems.

parameters.name: mglevels / gmglevels
parameters.description: Maximum number of algebraic levels (default 5) and the number of geometric multigrid levels.

parameters.name: Presmoother / Postsmoother
parameters.description: Created under feature("pr") and feature("po"); typical smoothers are SOR, SOR Vector (for vector elements), SCGS and Vanka (for saddle-point problems such as incompressible flow), and Incomplete LU.

parameters.name: Coarse Solver
parameters.description: Created under feature("cs"); usually a Direct solver, since the coarsest problem is small enough to factorize.

parameters.name: Administrative slots
parameters.description: feature("pr"), feature("po"), feature("cs"), plus feature("sso"), feature("ssso"), feature("ps") and feature("vs") for Schur, pressure and velocity solvers; they hold subfeatures and no settings of their own.

tools.notes: Geometric multigrid needs a mesh (or element-order) hierarchy: if a coarse level cannot be generated, COMSOL falls back and the solver slows down - reduce gmglevels or use AMG. Smoother choice is physics dependent: SOR Vector for curl-conforming (vector) elements in electromagnetics, Vanka or SCGS for incompressible flow saddle-point systems, plain SOR for scalar elliptic problems. Multigrid can also be used as the outer solver, not just as a preconditioner.

tools.name: Store Solution
tools.description: A placeholder feature in a solver sequence that stores a reference to a computed solution at that point in the sequence. It is how multi-step studies keep intermediate results (the prestressed state before an eigenfrequency solve, the last time step before a restart) and how a parametric sweep keeps one solution object per parameter set. Use getString("sol") to find the tag of the solver sequence that actually holds the stored data.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > right-click > Other > Store Solution; API: model.sol("sol1").create("su1", "StoreSolution")

parameters.name: sol
parameters.description: Read-only string naming the solver sequence that stores the solution; retrieved with feature(<ftag>).getString("sol").

parameters.name: Related methods
parameters.description: model.sol(<tag>).feature().tags() lists stored solutions after a sweep; getParamNames() and getParamVals() give the parameter values attached to each.

tools.notes: After a parametric sweep, model.batch(<pname>).feature(<fname>).getString("psol") gives the solver sequence holding all the swept solutions, and each Store Solution inside it points at one parameter's data. Storing many full 3D solutions is the usual reason .mph files become huge - set keepsol to last on the sweep when only the final state matters.

tools.name: Stop Condition
tools.description: An attribute that halts a time-dependent, time-explicit or parametric solve as soon as a condition is met, instead of running the full time or parameter list. The expression is evaluated after every step and the stepping stops when its real part goes negative; alternatively it stops when a given implicit event triggers. Use it to end a simulation when a temperature limit is reached, when a tank empties, when a solution stops changing, or to abort a run that is heading for divergence.
tools.usage: Study 1 > Solver Configurations > Solution 1 > Time-Dependent Solver 1 > right-click > Stop Condition; API: model.sol("sol1").feature("t1").create("st1", "StopCondition")

parameters.name: stopcondarr
parameters.description: Vector of stop-condition expressions; set entries with setIndex, e.g. setIndex("stopcondarr", "(1/timestep)<200", 1) for the second condition.

parameters.name: stopcondActive
parameters.description: Vector of "on"/"off" entries saying which conditions are currently active.

parameters.name: stopconddesc
parameters.description: Vector of descriptions shown next to each condition in the GUI.

parameters.name: Storage of the final step
parameters.description: The solution for which the expression is negative is not returned; the study extension settings control whether the steps before and after the trigger are kept.

tools.notes: Write the expression so it is positive while the run should continue and crosses zero at the stop point. The condition is only tested at solver steps, so with free time stepping it can overshoot - combine it with Intermediate stepping, or with an implicit Event, when the trigger instant must be accurate. Stop conditions can also be attached to a Parametric attribute to abort a sweep early.
